column3: Directly challenges worship of what can neither benefit nor harm, completing Ibrahim's incapacity test.
Commands believers to speak rightly, offering a general speech ethic for Ibrahim's address.
Recounts Ibrahim questioning his father and people about the idols to which they are devoted.
The father's hostile response is the immediate continuation of Ibrahim's appeal.
Ibrahim declares to his father and people that he is free of what they worship.
Links obedient speech to repaired deeds and forgiveness, but does not address false worship.
Reprises Ibrahim's question to his father and people about what they worship.

Again portrays Ibrahim asking his father and people what they worship.

The annunciation to Mary does not clarify Ibrahim's filial appeal.
Hearing God's word contrasts with devotion to objects incapable of hearing.
Moses's privileged call does not develop the focus's idol critique.

Unveiled sight at judgment is unrelated to the father's idolatry.

The sending of devils against disbelievers does not clarify the focus.

Noah's family correction concerns a different issue and does not develop the focus.
The calf cannot answer, harm, or benefit, closely matching Ibrahim's test of worshipped objects.
Shade that does not protect from flame is unrelated to the focus.
Denies that what is worshipped besides God can provide anything, reinforcing exclusive divine agency.
God gives hearing and sight, directly contrasting the faculties denied of the father's objects of worship.
Conjecture cannot avail against truth, but it does not concern devotional objects.
Jacob asks his sons whom they will worship, a meaningful family-and-worship parallel.
Mutual future seeing does not illuminate the focus.
God's gift of hearing and sight contrasts with the idols' total inability to possess either faculty.
Ibrahim's disavowal of false worship and his limited promise to his father closely parallel the focus's conflict.
God alone sees, hears, and governs, supplying the positive divine counterpart to the focus's negations.

The future command to watch concerns a different warning scene.
Given hearing and sight do not avail deniers, providing a limited contrast to false objects.

It rejects invoking what neither benefits nor harms and calls back to God's guidance.
Ibrahim's dispute with his people over association is related but lacks the filial address and incapacity test.

Concealed objectionable speech has no material relation to the focus.
Moses's reminder of favors does not develop the idol critique.

Judgment according to deeds does not bear on this appeal.

Human creation and resurrection do not clarify the filial idol critique.

Introduces Ibrahim as a truthful prophet immediately before his appeal to his father.
Questions worship of what cannot harm or benefit, directly restating the focus's criterion.
Ibrahim renounces association and turns wholly to the Creator, supplying the positive conclusion of his critique.
Ibrahim challenges fear of associated beings that lack any divine warrant, extending his anti-idolatry argument.
Security belongs to those who do not mix faith with association, stating the moral alternative to the father's worship.
Challenges association with beings that create nothing and are themselves created.
States that false gods cannot help their worshippers or even help themselves.
Says invoked beings besides God cannot help worshippers and cannot help themselves.
Condemns worship of what neither harms nor benefits and exposes false intercession claims.
False invocations cannot answer their callers, closely matching the focus's test of unresponsive objects.
Ibrahim prays that he and his descendants be kept from worshipping idols.
Ibrahim says the idols have led many astray, clarifying the danger he seeks to avert from his father.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created.
False gods are lifeless and unaware, reinforcing the focus's denial of their perception and agency.
Those called besides God cannot remove harm or alter it.
They take gods besides God for supposed strength, immediately setting up their failure in 19:82.
The calf is described as a body that merely produced a sound, exposing the inadequacy of the object worshipped.
Aaron warns his people against following the calf, a prophetic correction of false worship.
God gave Ibrahim sound judgment before his confrontation with his father and people over their idols.
Ibrahim's opponents admit that their idols cannot speak, a close parallel to the focus's incapacity test.
Ibrahim rebukes worship of what cannot benefit, calling his opponents to reason.
It condemns invoking what neither harms nor benefits, a direct general parallel to Ibrahim's argument.
Those invoked besides God cannot even create a fly or recover what it takes, demonstrating their helplessness.
False gods neither create nor control death, life, or resurrection.
Ibrahim's people answer that they worship idols, initiating the fuller version of his critique.
Ibrahim asks whether the idols hear when they are called, directly matching the focus's first question.
Ibrahim asks whether the idols benefit or harm, directly matching the focus's final criterion.
The people appeal to ancestral practice, clarifying the inherited worship that Ibrahim confronts in his father.
Ibrahim declares himself an enemy to all the objects they worship besides the Lord of the worlds.
Ibrahim tells his people that idols cannot provide for them and calls them to seek provision from God.
Those invoked besides God possess nothing in the heavens or earth and have no share in governance.
Invoked beings do not hear calls and, even if they heard, could not answer, an exceptionally close parallel.
People take gods besides God hoping for help, exposing the false reliance challenged in the focus.
False gods cannot help their worshippers, though the worshippers remain gathered in their service.
Ibrahim challenges his people for seeking fabricated gods besides God.
Ibrahim asks the idols why they do not speak, directly paralleling the focus's denial of responsiveness.
Ibrahim asks whether they worship what they themselves carve.
God created both the worshippers and what they make, grounding Ibrahim's rejection of idol worship.
It challenges reliance on beings besides God that cannot remove harm or withhold mercy.
The Prophet is forbidden to worship those invoked besides God after clear proofs have come.
Ibrahim makes the Creator alone the exception to his disavowal of what his father and people worship.
Challenges those invoked besides God to show what they have created or shared in creation.
No one is more astray than one who invokes beings that cannot answer until the Day of Resurrection.
